articles.title: Fairy Tale – The Lamia of Zarakies
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: Fairy tale from Zarakies, Euboea, about a Lamia who ate people, until the youngest brother managed to defeat her with the help of his dogs.

image.alt: Illustration of the Lamia from Euboea

content.value:
Once there was a mother who said:

- Let me have a daughter, and let her become a Lamia!

This mother had ten sons and no daughter, which is why she said this. So she gave birth to a girl, and she became a Lamia.

Afterwards, this Lamia would rise at night and eat the people of the village! She ate her brothers too. But the youngest, the very smallest, was clever. He fled from the house. She had also eaten their father, and their mother. He, the smallest of all, who was clever, escaped from the house and ran away.

He fled from the house. She had eaten their father, and their mother too. He, the smallest of all, who was clever, had escaped from the house and run away. He went and climbed high into three cypress trees. They were all in a row.

He had told his parents that she was eating people, but they did not believe him. Because she was their only daughter, they loved her, even though she was a Lamia.

Once she had eaten them all and only he was left, he still had the three dogs. But the dogs were tied up at the house. The child climbed into the first cypress tree. The Lamia had one great tooth — one tooth, and a huge one! She went and began gnawing at the cypress tree, scratch-scratch. The child leapt to the other cypress tree. The Lamia was there again.

The Lamia was there again.

When the child realized she would cut through that one too and only one was left, to get there in time he began calling out to the dogs:

- Come here, Azlanis! Come here, Kaplanis! Come here, little Lepuranis!

Then he climbed into the other cypress, the third one. Having climbed up, he called out again with all his might:

- Come here, Azlanis! Come here, Kaplanis! Come here, little Lepuranis!

The oldest of the dogs heard him and said:

- The master is calling us!

The others said:

- We have bigger ears than you and cannot hear him. How is it that you heard the master calling?

The dogs listened carefully and heard the master. They gathered their strength, snapped the rope, and went to where they heard the master's call.

They came there and he told them:

- Catch the Lamia and do not let a single drop of blood fall to the ground! Eat the Lamia whole.

The dogs seized the Lamia in their teeth and ate her whole, but three drops of blood fell. From the blood that spilled, all the people the Lamia had eaten came back to life.

And then they all found one another, embraced, kissed, and afterwards they lived happily, and we even more so.

articles.title: The Koutsocheria – Karytaina, Gortynia
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Traditional narrative of the appearance of the Koutsocheria in the waters of Karytaina

content.value: A woman saw within the river a creature dressed in red, with her hair spread out, combing it. She took her for a woman and called out to her. The creature immediately fell into the river and the waters swallowed her up. Then she understood that it had been the Koutsocheria, and she rose and fled.

articles.title: The Lamna of Koropi
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative of the Lamna that appeared in the well of Koropi and its destruction

content.value: In an old well at Koropi there appeared a Lamna that struck animals and sucked their blood. No one dared shoot it, for fear the bullet would rebound and kill them. But one day the Lamna struck the two oxen of a villager — his only property — and in his despair he seized his rifle, fired with his left hand, and killed the Lamna. Its body was three fathoms long. They threw it outside the village, onto a deserted plain, and wherever its blood dripped, no grass ever grew again.

articles.title: Definition of the Strigles – Nikolaos Politis
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk definition and description of the activities of the Strigles in Greek tradition

content.value: Strigles are poor and wretched old women who cannot do any good for a person, devoted entirely to magic. They do things that please the devil — powders, ointments, herbs, and suchlike. They do not trouble men much, but they do great harm to women and children, if these set any obstacle in the way of their magic; and with their breath and their blowing alone, they can either drive them mad or even kill them.

They go to newborn babies who are crying, and they suck their blood, leaving them withered. These children, even if they do not die, remain wretched and sickly all their lives. For this reason, before a child is baptized, it is never left alone. And if, before the Strigles have sucked all the child's blood, the parents realize the child is in danger from them, they drive them away with noises and clapping of hands. The Strigles, so as not to be caught, flee from the house.

Strigles dwell in the mountains and frequently come down to villages and towns. They run along the roads riding reeds, and breathe fire from their mouths. They have sharp claws, and they flay anyone they encounter on the road.

articles.title: The Strigles of Lasta – Gortynia
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative of three immortal Strigles and the sharing of their sense organs

content.value: The Strigles were three old women who never died. And they had one tooth, one ear, and one eye, which each one took in turn. But they were always quarreling and squabbling, because each wanted to have the eye to see, or at least the ear to hear. The tooth they rarely wanted, only to eat.

For this reason, often, because they could not agree, they hid them; and if anyone managed to steal them at such a moment, they would give him whatever he asked for. For from their craft as Strigles they had everything. But only one man managed to steal them, and they gave him whatever he asked.

articles.title: The Strigles of Mykonos
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk practice of frightening children with the threat of the Strigles of Mykonos

content.value: Most of the Strigles are found on Mykonos. For this reason, when a child cries incessantly, they scold it and say: "Why are you crying, little strigla? Shall we send you to Mykonos to join the other Strigles?"
"Sometimes, to frighten it, they say: "I will call the Strigles from Mykonos to take you!"

articles.title: The Strigla-Village – Messenia
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative of the nocturnal activities of the Strigles in Prasteio and the revelation of their identities

content.value: Prasteio is also called Striglochorion ('Strigla-Village') because many women in it were Strigles. Every night they went down to the shore at Selenitsa, where many ships were always moored; they would choose one, get on board, set the sails, and navigate like men. At dawn they would return, bringing sugar cane, for they had sailed as far as the places where it grows.

One young man happened to be sleeping one night inside the ship the Strigles boarded, without them noticing him. The Strigles, as soon as they stepped aboard the ship, undressed, set their clothes aside, with one taking the sails, another the helm, and they made their way.

When the young man came to his senses, he suspected what was afoot — for in his village they said there were some Strigles who every night made this voyage. Who they were he could not tell, but he used his wits and cut a piece from each woman's dress, which lay nearby.

They went and returned, with the young man still on the ship. But in the morning he wasted no time: he went to Prasteio and revealed the matter, and so the Strigles were identified. Their husbands watched them closely, but they always found a way, and every night at midnight they never missed the voyage. They say moreover that one of them ate her own child.

articles.title: Two Strigles – Thouria
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative of the encounter with two Strigles in Thouria, Messenia

content.value: A man from our village stayed one night at the house of his godfather, where there was no one else present but the two of them and the godfather's wife and mother-in-law. Around midnight he heard a commotion and woke up; he lay still listening, and heard the two women talking to each other. When he heard what they were saying, he was horrified, for they were plotting to eat that night the fatter of the two sleeping men.
He then understood that both the wife and mother-in-law of his godfather were Strigles, and he was wondering how to find some way to escape, for he realized he had no power to do anything to them.

The Strigles moved toward the two men who were lying down, and first took hold of the godfather's leg and lifted it. They wanted to see whether his leg was heavy, for that would show whether he was fat. But he understood their intention, and as they lifted his leg and weighed it in their hands, he lifted it himself too, so that it seemed to them as light as a feather, and they dropped it angrily.

They lifted the householder's leg as well, and as he was deep in sleep, they found it very heavy. Pleased with this, they immediately split open his chest, took out his liver and cast it on the coals to cook. Then they saw they had no wine, and flew off to a wine shop, helped themselves to as much as they wanted, and returned.

While they were away, however, the godfather rose up quickly, gathered the liver from the fire and hid it inside his shirt, putting in its place ashes from the coals. The Strigles ate with appetite what they found, but it seemed to them charred and tasteless.

In the morning both godfathers rose and left the house. The householder was yellow as a gold coin and felt great weakness, but his chest, which had been split open during the night, showed no sign. He told his godfather he was very hungry, and the latter gave him the cooked liver, which he ate, and it seemed to him very strengthening.

After a while his cheeks began to redden, and he became quite well. Then his friend told him everything that had happened during the night. And they went together to the house and killed the Strigles.

articles.title: The Mora in Athens
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk description of the Mora as a nocturnal Lamna who causes suffocation in people

content.value: The Mora is a Lamna — wealthy and very powerful. She walks only at night, and sometimes when she encounters people sleeping in her path, she sits on their chests and crushes them. She is so heavy that whoever she crushes groans like an ox.
But if the person is not deep in sleep and sees her and snatches her fez, then whatever he asks for — wealth and goods — she will give him, so long as he returns her fez.

articles.title: The Strigles of Rhodes
articles.author: Αναστάσιος Βρόντης
articles.excerpt: Legend of Strigles in Afantou, Rhodes who enter houses on the evenings of the Sarantaimero, strangle infants and cause miscarriages in pregnant women. Example: a coffee-shop owner from Fantenos lost a baby that could not sleep.

content.value:
In Afantou they say there are women who go about on the evenings of the Sarantaimero (the forty-day period) and enter other people's houses, strangling their infant children. They also cause pregnant women to miscarry.

A coffee-shop owner from Fantenos had an infant child, and every evening they would not let it sleep until they had strangled it.

articles.title: The Lamia–Dragon Connection – Study by George Frederick Abbott
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: Academic study on the relationship between the Lamia and the Dragon in Macedonian folklore: kinship or marriage, shared cannibalistic nature, origin of the proverb 'Eats like a Lamia', and classical references.

content.value: The Lamia is associated with the Dragon either through kinship or — very often — through the bonds of marriage. She fully shares with him her cannibalistic nature and her childlike simplicity. Her gluttony has given rise to the well-known proverb: 'Eats like a Lamia.'

Despite this ungenteel trait, she is of noble lineage and may boast of her presence in the pages of classical literature — although, it must be noted, the circumstances in which she appears are not exactly those a lady of her standing would wish to be remembered...

For instance, the scandalous episode of "hōs hē Lami' halous' ep' ergōi'" (Aristoph. Wasps 1177) appears to have been widely known in Athens in 422 BC, and one can easily imagine the laughter and cheers that the poet's allusion would have provoked in the theatre.
